A1: correct oblique asymptote equation stated
A1: correct vertical asymptote(s) also stated

common_errors.description: Concluding 'no horizontal asymptote' as the final word without checking for the oblique case
Long division error producing an incorrect linear quotient

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine whether the graph of a rational function crosses its horizontal or oblique asymptote at any finite x, correcting the misconception that it never can.
question_archetypes.example: Show that g(x)=(x^4+x^2)/(x^4+1) crosses its horizontal asymptote y=1.
question_archetypes.answer: Setting g(x)=1 gives x^2=1, i.e. x=+/-1 are finite points where the graph meets y=1 — the asymptote describes only end behavior (x->+/-infinity), not a barrier the graph can never touch.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly asks whether the curve crosses its own asymptote — a conceptual archetype correcting the common misconception that asymptotes can never be crossed.
method_plan: Set f(x) equal to the asymptote's equation (y=L or y=ax+b)
Solve for any finite x satisfying this equation
If solutions exist, conclude the graph crosses the asymptote there
Explain that asymptotic behavior only concerns the limit as x->+/-infinity, not intermediate values
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct equation set up (f(x)=asymptote)
A1: correct solution(s) for the crossing point(s)
A1: correct conceptual explanation of why crossing is allowed

common_errors.description: Believing a curve can never cross its horizontal/oblique asymptote
Error solving the resulting polynomial equation for the crossing point

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Determine that a rational function has NO horizontal or oblique asymptote because the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's by more than 1.
question_archetypes.example: Show that f(x)=x^4/(x+1) has no horizontal or oblique asymptote.
question_archetypes.answer: deg(numerator)=4, deg(denominator)=1, difference is 3>1, so f grows without a linear (or constant) end behavior — no horizontal or oblique asymptote exists (only a vertical one at x=-1)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The degree gap between numerator and denominator is 2 or more — students often try to force a horizontal or oblique asymptote where none exists.
method_plan: Compare deg(numerator) to deg(denominator)
If the gap exceeds 1, state that no horizontal or oblique asymptote exists
Still find any vertical asymptotes from the denominator's zeros
State the end behavior qualitatively if requested (e.g. f -> +/-infinity like a polynomial of the quotient's degree)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct degree comparison showing the gap exceeds 1
A1: correct conclusion of no horizontal/oblique asymptote
A1: correct vertical asymptote(s) still identified

common_errors.description: Attempting long division and reporting a linear 'oblique asymptote' even though the remainder does not vanish at infinity
Failing to still report the vertical asymptote(s) that DO exist

micro_skills.topic: Sketching the Graph of a Function
micro_skills.micro_skill: Assemble domain, asymptotes, symmetry, sign charts of f' and f'' into a complete, correctly labeled sketch

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a rational function, work through the full checklist (domain, asymptotes, symmetry, intercepts, f' sign chart, f'' sign chart) and describe/sketch the complete graph.
question_archetypes.answer: Vertical asymptotes x=+/-2, horizontal y=1, even function, intercepts (0,1/4),(+/-1,0); f'(x)=-6x/(x^2-4)^2 gives a single local max at x=0 (f(0)=1/4); f''(x)=6(3x^2+4)/(x^2-4)^3 gives concave up for |x|>2, concave down for |x|<2, with no interior inflection (concavity only switches across the asymptotes)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks to 'sketch' or fully describe a function rather than compute a single quantity — signals that ALL of domain/asymptotes/symmetry/f'/f'' must be assembled systematically, in the standard checklist order.
method_plan: Compute f' and f'' in fully factored form
From f: state domain, asymptotes, symmetry (even/odd), intercepts
From f': find critical/singular points, build sign chart, classify local extrema
From f'': find zeros, build sign chart, identify concavity and true inflection points
Assemble all information into a coherent description/sketch
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct domain, asymptotes, symmetry, intercepts
M1: correct f' sign chart and extrema classification
M1: correct f'' sign chart and concavity/inflection points
A1: all pieces correctly assembled into one coherent sketch/description

common_errors.description: Computing f' and f'' correctly but never assembling them with the asymptote/symmetry information into one coherent picture
Reporting a concavity change 'at' a vertical asymptote as if it were an inflection point (inflection requires a point actually ON the graph)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Sketch a non-rational function combining a polynomial factor with an exponential decay term (e.g. x*e^(-x^2/2)), identifying horizontal asymptotes from limiting behavior rather than a degree comparison.
question_archetypes.example: Sketch y=x*e^(-x^2/2).
question_archetypes.answer: Domain all reals; odd function; horizontal asymptote y=0 both directions (exponential decay beats the linear factor); y'=(1-x^2)e^(-x^2/2), critical points x=+/-1 (local min at -1, local max at 1); y''=x(x^2-3)e^(-x^2/2), inflections at x=0,+/-sqrt(3)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is not rational (contains e^(-x^2) or similar decay), so the degree-comparison asymptote rules don't apply directly — horizontal asymptotes must be argued from limiting behavior (exponential beats polynomial), and symmetry (odd/even) is often a useful shortcut.
method_plan: Determine domain and check for odd/even symmetry
Argue horizontal asymptote(s) from limiting behavior (exponential decay dominates polynomial growth)
Find f' and f'' via product/chain rule, build sign charts
Assemble critical points, inflection points, and asymptotic behavior into a full sketch
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct domain and symmetry
M1: correct horizontal-asymptote argument via limiting behavior
M1: correct f' and f'' sign charts with correct critical/inflection points
A1: complete, coherent assembled sketch

common_errors.description: Trying to apply the rational-function degree-comparison rule to a transcendental function
Product/chain rule error computing y' or y'' for the exponential term

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Sketch an odd rational function with two vertical asymptotes symmetric about the origin, using symmetry to halve the required work.
question_archetypes.example: Sketch f(x)=x/(x^2-1).
question_archetypes.answer: Domain x≠+/-1; odd function; vertical asymptotes x=+/-1; horizontal asymptote y=0; f'(x)=-(x^2+1)/(x^2-1)^2<0 everywhere in the domain (always decreasing, no local extrema); f''(x)=2x(x^2+3)/(x^2-1)^3 gives one inflection point at x=0 (the others are asymptotes, not domain points)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is odd (f(-x)=-f(x)) — symmetry lets you analyze only x>0 and reflect, halving the work; watch for zeros of f'' that coincide with points OUTSIDE the domain (near asymptotes), which are not true inflection points.
method_plan: Verify odd symmetry and note domain restrictions from the denominator
Analyze f' and f'' fully (or just for x>0 and reflect by symmetry)
Distinguish zeros of f'' that lie in the domain (true inflection candidates) from sign changes that occur only across an asymptote
Assemble the full sketch using symmetry to double-check
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct symmetry and domain identified
M1: correct f' and f'' analysis (using symmetry where helpful)
A1: correct identification of the one true interior inflection point
A1: coherent final sketch assembled

common_errors.description: Treating a concavity switch across a vertical asymptote as an inflection point on the graph
Not exploiting odd symmetry, doing twice the necessary sign-chart work

micro_skills.micro_skill: Optimize area/perimeter given a fixed amount of fencing or material, including the one-side-free variant
definitions: Optimization procedure: (1) identify the quantity Q to optimize, (2) sketch, (3) define symbols, (4) express Q as a function of the relevant variable(s), (5) find constraint equation(s), (6) reduce Q to a function of ONE variable with a determined valid interval, (7) find the extreme value (critical/singular points AND endpoints), (8) state the conclusion in context.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: A rectangular enclosure uses an existing wall as one side (fencing needed on only three sides); maximize the area given a fixed total fence length.
question_archetypes.example: A rectangular enclosure uses an existing wall as one side; the other three sides use 100 m of fence. Maximize the area.
question_archetypes.answer: Max area 1250 m^2 at y=25 (perpendicular sides), x=50 (side parallel to wall)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The phrase 'existing wall as one side' or 'no fence needed on one side' signals the constraint uses only 3 sides of fencing (x+2y=L), not the usual 4-sided perimeter, changing the coefficient in the constraint equation.
method_plan: Define x = side parallel to the wall, y = each perpendicular side
Write the fencing constraint x+2y=L and solve for x in terms of y
Substitute into A=xy to get A as a function of y alone, with 0<=y<=L/2
Find the critical point of A(y), compare to A at endpoints (which are 0), and state the maximum in context
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct 3-sided constraint equation
M1: correct single-variable area function and its valid domain
A1: correct critical point and comparison confirming it's a maximum
A1: final answer stated in context with both dimensions

common_errors.description: Using the usual 4-sided perimeter formula (2x+2y=L) instead of the 3-sided one
Failing to restrict the domain of y to physically meaningful values, so the endpoint comparison (needed to confirm a max, not just a critical point) is skipped

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Maximize the area of a rectangle given a fixed standard (4-sided) perimeter.
question_archetypes.example: A rectangle has perimeter 60 m. Find the dimensions that maximize its area.
question_archetypes.answer: x=y=15 m (a square), maximum area 225 m^2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A standard perimeter constraint (fencing on all four sides, or simply 'perimeter is P') — the baseline case establishing that the optimal rectangle for fixed perimeter is always a square.
method_plan: Write the constraint 2x+2y=P and solve for y in terms of x
Substitute into A=xy to get a single-variable function on 0<x<P/2
Find the critical point and confirm it is a maximum (compare to boundary behavior, both giving A->0)
State the dimensions and maximum area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct constraint and substitution
M1: correct critical point found
A1: correct confirmation of maximum via boundary/endpoint behavior
A1: correct final dimensions and area

common_errors.description: Sign or substitution error solving the constraint for y
Not verifying the critical point is a maximum (e.g. skipping the boundary check)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Maximize total area for two or more adjacent rectangular enclosures sharing a common internal fence, given a fixed total amount of fencing.
question_archetypes.example: A rectangular field is divided into two equal pens by a fence parallel to one side. If 240 m of fencing is available in total, maximize the total enclosed area.
question_archetypes.answer: With x=width shared by the dividing fence and y=length: constraint 2x+3y=240 (three vertical segments including the divider, two horizontal); maximize A=xy, giving x=60, y=40, area=2400 m^2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The phrase 'divided into pens' or 'internal fence' signals an extra fence segment must be added to the constraint equation beyond the usual outer perimeter — miscounting the number of fence segments is the main trap.
method_plan: Carefully count every fence segment (outer sides AND internal dividers) to build the correct linear constraint
Solve the constraint for one variable and substitute into the area (or total area) formula
Find the critical point of the resulting single-variable function
Confirm it's a maximum and state both dimensions and the total area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct constraint equation accounting for ALL fence segments including internal dividers
M1: correct reduction to a single-variable area function
A1: correct critical point found and confirmed as maximum
A1: correct final dimensions and total area

common_errors.description: Forgetting to include the internal dividing fence segment(s) in the total fencing constraint
Arithmetic error solving the resulting linear constraint for the substitution variable

micro_skills.subtopic: Box/Volume Optimization from a Sheet or Fixed Volume
micro_skills.micro_skill: Optimize the volume (or surface area) of a box built from a flat sheet or with a fixed-volume constraint

question_archetypes.prompt_template: An open-top box is formed by cutting equal squares from the corners of a rectangular sheet and folding up the sides; maximize the resulting volume.
question_archetypes.example: A box with no top is made from a 70 cm x 150 cm sheet by cutting equal squares of side x from each corner. Maximize the volume.
question_archetypes.answer: x=15 cm gives maximum volume V=72,000 cm^3 (the other critical point x≈58.33 is rejected as outside the valid domain 0<x<35)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The phrase 'cut equal squares from each corner and fold up the sides' is the defining cue for this specific construction — the resulting cubic volume function must be restricted to a valid domain (0<x<half the shorter side) before finding the extremum.
method_plan: Express the resulting base dimensions as (L-2x) and (W-2x), height x
Write V(x)=x(L-2x)(W-2x) and determine the valid domain of x
Differentiate, solve V'(x)=0, and discard any root outside the valid domain
Confirm the remaining critical point is a maximum by checking V=0 at both endpoints
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct volume function V(x) with correct domain restriction
M1: correct derivative and quadratic/cubic solved for critical points
A1: correctly rejects any root outside the valid domain
A1: correct final maximum volume and value of x

common_errors.description: Not restricting the domain of x, so an algebraically valid but physically impossible root is accepted
Expansion error forming the cubic V(x)=4x^3-... from the product of three factors

question_archetypes.prompt_template: A closed rectangular box with a square base must have a given fixed volume; minimize its total surface area.
question_archetypes.example: A closed rectangular box with a square base is to have volume 32 m^3. Minimize the total surface area.
question_archetypes.answer: x=32^(1/3)≈3.17 m (base side), y≈3.17 m (height, equal to x — a cube), S_min≈60.6 m^2
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A fixed VOLUME constraint (not perimeter/fence) together with a request to minimize surface area — use the volume equation to eliminate one variable (typically height) before differentiating S.
method_plan: Let x=base side, y=height; write V=x^2 y=(given constant) and solve for y in terms of x
Substitute into S=2x^2+4xy to get S as a function of x alone, x>0
Argue existence of a minimum via boundary limits (S->infinity as x->0+ or x->infinity)
Find the critical point, confirm minimum, state dimensions and minimum surface area
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct elimination of y using the volume constraint
M1: correct S(x) and its derivative
A1: correct existence argument and critical point
A1: correct final dimensions and minimum surface area

common_errors.description: Substitution error eliminating y from the volume constraint
Skipping the existence-of-minimum argument (boundary limits) before trusting the critical point

question_archetypes.prompt_template: A closed box has a fixed volume, but different faces (e.g. base vs. sides) cost different amounts per unit area; minimize total cost rather than plain surface area.
question_archetypes.example: A closed box with a square base has volume 50 m^3. The base and top cost $2/m^2, the sides cost $1/m^2. Minimize the total material cost.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Per-unit-area COSTS differing between faces (not just total surface area) are given — each face's area must be weighted by its own cost coefficient before summing into a single cost function.
method_plan: Identify each distinct face type (base, top, sides) and its area formula and cost per unit area
Use the volume constraint to eliminate one variable
Form the total cost function as the weighted sum of face areas x costs
Differentiate, find critical point, confirm minimum, state dimensions and minimum cost
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification and area formula for each distinct face type
M1: correct weighted cost function with the volume constraint substituted in
A1: correct critical point found and confirmed as a minimum
A1: correct final minimum cost stated

common_errors.description: Using plain surface area instead of weighting each face by its distinct cost per unit area
Error combining the base/top cost terms (forgetting the base and top are two separate faces of equal area)

micro_skills.micro_skill: Optimize the shape (dimensions) of a cylindrical or other curved container for minimum material given fixed volume
formulas: S=2 pi r h + 2 pi r^2 (cylinder total surface area)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the most economical shape (minimum surface area for a given fixed volume) of a closed cylindrical can.
question_archetypes.example: Find the most economical shape (minimum surface area for given volume V) of a cylindrical can.
question_archetypes.answer: h=2r (height equals diameter) at the minimum, where r^3=V/(2*pi)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A cylindrical container with a fixed volume and a request to minimize total surface area (or material cost) — classic setup where eliminating h via V=pi r^2 h leaves a single-variable function of r with a 2V/r + 2 pi r^2 shape.
method_plan: Write V=pi r^2 h (constant) and solve for h in terms of r
Substitute into S=2 pi r h + 2 pi r^2 to get S(r) = 2V/r + 2 pi r^2
Argue a minimum exists via boundary limits as r->0+ and r->infinity
Differentiate, solve S'(r)=0, and express the result as a relation between h and r
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct elimination of h using the volume constraint
M1: correct S(r) and its derivative
A1: correct existence argument and critical point solved
A1: correct final relation h=2r stated clearly

common_errors.description: Sign or algebra error solving S'(r)=0 for r^3
Leaving the answer purely numeric without stating the elegant relation h=2r (diameter=height)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Same cylindrical-can setup but with NO top (open cylinder), changing the surface-area formula and hence the optimal ratio between height and radius.
question_archetypes.example: Find the most economical shape of an open-topped cylindrical can (no lid) with fixed volume V.
question_archetypes.answer: S(r)=V/r... specifically S=2 pi r h + pi r^2 with h=V/(pi r^2) substituted gives S(r)=2V/r+pi r^2; S'(r)=-2V/r^2+2 pi r=0 => r^3=V/pi, giving h=r (height equals radius, not 2r)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem specifies 'no lid' or 'open top' — the surface area formula changes (only one circular face, pi r^2 instead of 2 pi r^2), which changes the optimal ratio from h=2r to h=r; a strong distractor for students who memorize the closed-can ratio.
method_plan: Write the correct open-cylinder surface area S=2 pi r h + pi r^2 (only one flat face)
Eliminate h using the volume constraint
Differentiate and solve for the critical point
State the resulting height-to-radius ratio, contrasting with the closed-can case
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct open-cylinder surface area formula (only one circular face)
M1: correct elimination and differentiation
A1: correct critical point solved
A1: correct final ratio h=r stated, distinguishing it from the closed-can result

common_errors.description: Reusing the closed-cylinder surface area formula (with 2 pi r^2) for an open-top can
Misremembering the resulting ratio as h=2r from the closed case without re-deriving it

question_archetypes.prompt_template: A cylindrical container has fixed volume, but the circular ends and curved side are made of materials with different costs per unit area; minimize total cost.
question_archetypes.example: A cylindrical can of fixed volume V has ends costing twice as much per unit area as the curved side. Find the dimensions minimizing total cost.
question_archetypes.answer: Cost C(r,h)=2(2*pi r^2)*k + (2 pi r h)*(k) for some unit cost k, with h eliminated via V=pi r^2 h; differentiating gives a different optimal ratio than the equal-cost case (h=4r rather than h=2r)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Different costs per unit area for different faces of a curved container — analogous to the box-with-differing-face-costs archetype, but here the geometry is circular (curved side vs. flat ends).
method_plan: Identify the cost-per-area for each distinct face (ends vs. curved side)
Use the volume constraint to eliminate h
Form the weighted total cost function of r alone
Differentiate, solve for the critical point, and state the resulting optimal ratio
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct weighted cost function set up with distinct per-face costs
M1: correct elimination of h via the volume constraint
A1: correct critical point solved
A1: correct final dimensions/ratio stated

common_errors.description: Treating all faces as equal cost, ignoring the given cost weighting
Error differentiating the weighted cost function due to the extra constant factors

micro_skills.micro_skill: Minimize a distance (point-to-curve) or a path length/time, including angle-parametrized setups
definitions: Minimizing distance is often easier via D^2 (avoiding the square root) since D^2 and D are minimized at the same point (D>=0).

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find the point on a given curve closest to a fixed point not on the curve, minimizing D^2 instead of D.
question_archetypes.example: Find the point on the parabola y=x^2 closest to the point (0,3).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks for the closest point on a curve to a given fixed point — square the distance formula to avoid a square-root derivative, since minimizing D^2 gives the same critical points as minimizing D.
method_plan: Write D^2 = (x-a)^2+(y-b)^2 with y expressed via the curve's equation, giving a function of one variable
Differentiate D^2 with respect to that variable and set to zero
Solve for the critical point(s), checking each against boundary/endpoint behavior if the domain is restricted
State the point(s) achieving the minimum distance
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct D^2 expressed as a function of one variable using the curve's equation
M1: correct derivative and critical point(s) solved
A1: correct minimum confirmed (e.g. via second derivative or boundary comparison)
A1: correct final point(s) stated

common_errors.description: Differentiating D (with the square root) directly instead of the simpler D^2
Sign/arithmetic error solving the resulting critical-point equation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Minimize a path length (e.g. a ladder reaching over an obstacle) by parametrizing with an angle theta rather than a linear distance.
question_archetypes.example: Find the shortest ladder that reaches from the ground, over a 2 m fence standing 1 m from a wall, to the wall.
question_archetypes.answer: L(theta) = 1/cos(theta) + 2/sin(theta), minimized where tan^3(theta)=2, giving L_min=(1+2^(2/3))^(3/2) ≈ 4.16 m
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The geometry naturally involves an angle (a ladder leaning at angle theta over an obstacle) rather than a single linear distance — parametrizing by theta on (0, pi/2) is far cleaner than by a linear variable.
method_plan: Define theta as the angle the ladder makes with the ground (or similar) and express L as a function of theta using right-triangle trig
Argue a minimum exists since L->infinity at both ends of (0,pi/2)
Differentiate L(theta), set to zero, and solve for tan(theta) or a related quantity
Substitute back using a Pythagorean identity to find L_min in closed form
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct trig setup for L(theta) using the given obstacle dimensions
M1: correct existence argument for a minimum on the open interval
M1: correct differentiation and critical equation solved
A1: correct final minimum length in exact/simplified form

common_errors.description: Attempting a linear-distance parametrization that leads to a much messier constraint equation than the angle-based one
Error converting the critical equation (e.g. tan^3(theta)=2) back into a closed-form length using sec^2=1+tan^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Minimize the total length of a path connecting a fixed point to another fixed point via an intermediate point constrained to lie on a given line or curve (e.g. a pipeline or road problem).
question_archetypes.example: A pipeline must run from a point A, 3 km from a straight river bank, to a point B on the opposite side 5 km downstream and 2 km from the bank, crossing the river perpendicular to the bank at some point P. Minimize total pipeline length (assuming a straight-line path on each side).
question_archetypes.answer: Let x=distance along the bank from the point nearest A to P: total length T(x)=sqrt(9+x^2)+sqrt(4+(5-x)^2); T'(x)=0 gives x/sqrt(9+x^2)=(5-x)/sqrt(4+(5-x)^2), solved numerically or via similar-triangle reasoning for the optimal x
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A single point P is free to move along a line/curve while both endpoints A, B are fixed off that line — sum of two square-root distance terms, each a function of the same single variable x, is the signature setup.
method_plan: Define x as the position of the free point P along the line
Express each leg's length via the Pythagorean/distance formula in terms of x
Sum the two legs into a single total-length function T(x)
Differentiate, set T'(x)=0, and solve (numerically if needed), checking the result against endpoint values
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct expression for each leg's length in terms of x
M1: correct total length function and its derivative
A1: correct critical point solved or set up correctly for numerical solution
A1: correct final minimum length or optimal position stated, checked against endpoints

common_errors.description: Fixing the position of P using a ratio guess instead of deriving it from T'(x)=0
Error differentiating one of the square-root distance terms via the chain rule

micro_skills.micro_skill: Recognize when the true optimum occurs at an endpoint (or a comparison is needed), not automatically at the interior critical point
definitions: A critical point of the objective function is not automatically the desired extremum — it may be a local minimum when a maximum is wanted (or vice versa), or an endpoint may give a better value; always compare.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Set up an optimization problem where the interior critical point actually gives the WORST (not best) value, and the true optimum is at an endpoint of the parameter's domain.
question_archetypes.example: A man who runs twice as fast as he swims stands at A on a circular pool of diameter 40 m and wants to reach the diametrically opposite point B fastest by running along the arc to C then swimming straight to B. Where should C be?
question_archetypes.answer: The interior critical point theta=pi/3 gives t≈45.11/k, actually the worst (a local MAX of time); the endpoint theta=pi (run the whole way) gives t=10*pi/k≈31.4/k, the true minimum time.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: After finding the critical point and computing its value, that value looks suspiciously large/unfavorable compared to a quick sanity check at an endpoint — this is the signal to always compare critical-point values against endpoint values before declaring victory.
method_plan: Set up the objective function (e.g. total time) in terms of one parameter over its full valid domain
Find all interior critical points and evaluate the objective there
ALSO evaluate the objective at every endpoint of the domain
Compare all values and select the true extremum, even if it's an endpoint rather than the critical point
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct objective function set up over the full domain
M1: correct critical point(s) found and evaluated
A1: correct endpoint value(s) also evaluated
A1: correct identification that the endpoint (not the critical point) gives the true optimum, with justification

common_errors.description: Assuming the interior critical point must be the answer without comparing to endpoint values
Misclassifying the critical point's nature (max vs min) without checking against the rest of the domain

question_archetypes.prompt_template: An optimization problem where the algebraically ideal critical point falls outside the physically valid domain, forcing the true optimum to occur at a domain endpoint.
question_archetypes.example: A rectangular banner's design constraint forces a variable x to satisfy 2<=x<=6, but the unrestricted optimization of the area function gives a critical point at x=8; find the true maximum on the valid domain.
question_archetypes.answer: Since x=8 is outside [2,6], evaluate the area function at the endpoints x=2 and x=6 instead; whichever gives the larger value is the true maximum on the restricted domain.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: Solving the derivative-equals-zero equation gives a value that violates a stated physical/domain restriction — the correct response is to discard it and check the restricted domain's endpoints directly, not to 'round' the critical point into range.
method_plan: Determine the physically valid domain of the variable from the problem's constraints
Find the critical point(s) of the objective function algebraically
Discard any critical point outside the valid domain
Evaluate the objective at the domain's endpoints (and any valid interior critical points) and select the true extremum
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct valid domain identified from the problem's physical constraints
M1: correct critical point(s) found, with the invalid one correctly discarded
A1: correct evaluation at the domain endpoints
A1: correct final extremum identified from the valid candidates

common_errors.description: Using an out-of-domain critical point anyway because it 'solves the equation'
Not stating the valid domain explicitly before evaluating candidates

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain, in general terms, why every single-variable optimization problem over a closed interval requires comparing endpoint values against critical-point values before concluding.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why, even after finding and classifying a critical point as a local maximum, a student should still check the endpoints of the problem's valid domain before stating the final answer.
question_archetypes.answer: A local maximum found via the derivative test is only guaranteed to be the best value in its immediate neighborhood; Theorem 5/6 guarantee the ABSOLUTE extremum exists somewhere among the critical points and endpoints together, so only a full comparison — not the local classification alone — can identify the true global optimum.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks for a general conceptual justification (why compare at all) rather than a specific numeric optimization — testing understanding of the difference between a local extremum and the absolute extremum on a bounded domain.
method_plan: State that the First/Second Derivative Tests only classify LOCAL behavior at a critical point
Recall that Theorem 5 guarantees an absolute extremum exists among critical points, singular points, and endpoints together
Conclude that comparing ALL candidate values is the only way to identify which one is the absolute extremum
Give a concrete contrasting example if requested
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct statement that derivative tests only establish local behavior
M1: correct reference to the theorem guaranteeing the absolute extremum lies among all candidates
A1: correct concluding statement tying local vs. absolute together

common_errors.description: Conflating 'local maximum' with 'the answer to the optimization problem' without the comparison step
Giving a vague answer without referencing the specific theorem guaranteeing where absolute extrema occur

micro_skills.micro_skill: Build the linearization L(x) of f about a, approximate f(x), and bound/sign the resulting error
definitions: The linearization of f about a is L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a) (the tangent-line equation), and f(x)≈L(x) for x near a.

theorems.name: Theorem 11 (error formula)
theorems.statement: If f'' exists on an interval containing a,x, the error E(x)=f(x)-L(x) satisfies E(x) = f''(s)/2 * (x-a)^2 for some s between a and x.
conditions: f'' exists on the interval containing a and x

formulas: Corollary A: if f'' has constant sign between a,x, E(x) has that same sign (concave up => f(x)>L(x); concave down => f(x)<L(x))
Corollary C: if M<f''(t)<N throughout, L(x)+(M/2)(x-a)^2 < f(x) < L(x)+(N/2)(x-a)^2

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Approximate f(x) near a known point a using the linearization L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a).
question_archetypes.example: Approximate sqrt(26) using linearization about x=25.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The target value (26) is close to a 'nice' value (25) where f and f' are easy to evaluate exactly — signals building the tangent-line approximation rather than computing directly.
method_plan: Choose a nearby point a where f(a) and f'(a) are easy to compute exactly
Write L(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)
Evaluate L at the target x
State the approximation
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct f(a) and f'(a)
A1: correct linearization formula written
A1: correct numeric approximation

common_errors.description: Choosing a nearby point a where f'(a) is not actually easy to evaluate exactly, defeating the purpose
Arithmetic slip evaluating L at the target x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: After linearizing, determine the SIGN of the approximation error using the sign of f'', and bound its magnitude using a bound K on |f''| over the relevant interval.
question_archetypes.example: For the sqrt(26) approximation about x=25, determine whether the estimate over- or under-shoots the true value, and bound the error.
question_archetypes.answer: f''(x)=-(1/4)x^(-3/2)<0 on (25,26), so the error is negative (true value is LESS than L, i.e. sqrt(26)<5.1); |f''(t)|<=1/500 for t>=25, so |E|<(1/2)(1/500)(1)^2=0.001, giving sqrt(26) in (5.099,5.1)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question explicitly asks to determine whether the approximation over- or under-estimates AND/OR to bound the error — requires both Corollary A (sign) and Corollary B (magnitude), using the MAXIMUM of |f''| over the whole interval between a and x, not just at a.
method_plan: Compute f''(x) and determine its sign on the interval between a and the target x
Apply Corollary A to state whether the approximation over- or under-estimates
Find a bound K on |f''| valid over the ENTIRE interval (not just at the endpoint a)
Apply Corollary B to bound |E(x)|, and state the resulting interval containing the true value
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct sign of f'' on the interval and correct over/under conclusion
M1: correct bound K valid over the whole interval (not just at a)
A1: correct error bound computed via Corollary B
A1: correct final interval containing the true value stated

common_errors.description: Using K=|f''(a)| instead of the maximum of |f''| over the entire interval between a and x
Omitting the sign determination, leaving only a magnitude bound without stating over- vs. under-estimate

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Approximate a trigonometric value not at a standard angle by linearizing about the nearest standard angle, and bound the error.
question_archetypes.example: Approximate cos(36°)=cos(pi/5) using linearization about pi/6; bound the error.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A trig value at a non-standard angle is requested, but a nearby standard angle (pi/6, pi/4, pi/3, etc.) is close by — linearize about the standard angle rather than attempting exact computation.
method_plan: Identify the nearest standard angle a with known exact f(a), f'(a)
Write L(x) and evaluate at the target angle (in radians)
Determine the sign of the error via f''
Bound the error magnitude using a bound on |f''| over the interval
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct standard angle chosen and exact f(a), f'(a)
M1: correct linearization evaluated at the target (with correct radian conversion)
A1: correct sign of the error
A1: correct error bound and resulting interval

common_errors.description: Forgetting to convert the angle difference to radians before using it in L(x)
Omitting the error-bound portion when the question explicitly asks for it

micro_skills.micro_skill: Use the differential dy=f'(x)dx to estimate a small change in a physical quantity
definitions: The differential approximation delta(y) ≈ dy = f'(x) dx estimates the change in y=f(x) resulting from a small change dx in x.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Estimate the change in a geometric quantity (volume, area) resulting from a small change in a linear dimension, using the differential rather than recomputing exactly.
question_archetypes.example: A spherical balloon's radius grows from 20.00 cm to 20.20 cm. Estimate the change in volume.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: A SMALL change in a linear dimension is given, and the change in a derived quantity (volume, area) is wanted — the differential approximation avoids recomputing V at both radii and subtracting.
method_plan: Identify the formula V=f(r) (or similar) and compute f'(r)
Write Delta V ≈ f'(r) Delta r
Substitute the base value of r and the small change Delta r
State the estimated change with units
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivative f'(r)
M1: correct differential formula set up
A1: correct numeric estimate with units

common_errors.description: Computing the exact change f(r+Delta r)-f(r) instead of using the differential shortcut when the differential is what's asked for
Arithmetic slip evaluating f'(r) at the base radius

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a percent (relative) error in a measured quantity, use differentials to estimate the resulting percent error in a derived quantity.
question_archetypes.example: The radius of a sphere is measured with a possible error of 2%. Estimate the resulting percent error in the computed volume.
question_archetypes.answer: dV/V = 3 dr/r (from V=(4/3)pi r^3, taking logarithmic differentiation or direct ratio), so a 2% error in r gives approximately 6% error in V
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem is phrased in terms of PERCENT or RELATIVE error rather than an absolute change — take the ratio dQ/Q (often via d(ln Q)) rather than computing an absolute differential.
method_plan: Express the derived quantity's differential dQ in terms of dr
Form the ratio dQ/Q and simplify to find the relative-error relationship (e.g. dV/V = 3 dr/r for a cube-power formula)
Substitute the given percent error in r
State the resulting percent error in Q
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct differential dQ set up
M1: correct relative-error ratio dQ/Q derived

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Estimate the change in an implicitly-defined quantity using differentials on both sides of a governing equation (a differential-form analogue of related rates).
question_archetypes.example: For the ideal-gas-like relation PV=k (k constant), if P increases by a small amount dP, estimate the resulting change dV in V.
question_archetypes.answer: Differentiating PV=k: P dV + V dP = 0, so dV = -(V/P) dP
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The governing relation links two quantities implicitly (not solved explicitly for one in terms of the other) — differentiate the whole equation (as with related rates, but using differentials 'd' instead of rates 'd/dt') to relate the small changes.
method_plan: Differentiate the governing equation implicitly, replacing d/dt-style rates with differentials d(...)
Solve the resulting linear relation for the differential of the quantity of interest
Substitute known values for the other quantities and the given small change
State the estimated change
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct implicit differentiation into differential form
M1: correct algebraic solve for the desired differential
A1: correct numeric estimate given the substituted values

common_errors.description: Attempting to solve the governing equation explicitly for one variable before differentiating, when implicit differentiation is more direct
Sign error solving the linear relation for the desired differential

micro_skills.subtopic: Constructing Taylor Polynomials and Bounding the Remainder
micro_skills.micro_skill: Construct P_n(x) by direct differentiation and bound the error using the Lagrange remainder
definitions: The nth-order Taylor polynomial of f about a is P_n(x)=f(a)+f'(a)(x-a)+...+f^(n)(a)/n! * (x-a)^n, matching f and its first n derivatives at x=a (Taylor polynomials about 0 are called Maclaurin polynomials).

theorems.name: Theorem 12 (Taylor's Theorem with Lagrange remainder)
theorems.statement: If f^(n+1) exists on an interval containing a,x, then f(x)=P_n(x)+E_n(x), where E_n(x) = f^(n+1)(s)/(n+1)! * (x-a)^(n+1) for some s between a and x.
conditions: f^(n+1) exists on the interval containing a and x

formulas: E_n(x) = f^(n+1)(s)/(n+1)! * (x-a)^(n+1), s between a and x

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Construct P_n(x) for a given f about a specified point a by directly computing successive derivatives.
question_archetypes.example: Find P_2(x) for f(x)=sqrt(x) about x=25, and use it to approximate sqrt(26).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem requests a Taylor polynomial of a SPECIFIC finite order n (not the general series) about a given point where derivatives can be computed directly — the direct-differentiation approach is expected.
method_plan: Compute f(a), f'(a), f''(a), ..., up to f^(n)(a)
Assemble P_n(x) = sum of f^(k)(a)/k! * (x-a)^k
Evaluate P_n at the target x if an approximation is requested
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct derivatives computed up to order n
M1: correct assembly of P_n(x) with correct factorial coefficients
A1: correct numeric approximation if requested

common_errors.description: Missing or incorrect factorial denominators (e.g. forgetting the 2! in the quadratic term)
Stopping the differentiation one order too early or too late relative to what n requires

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Bound the error in a degree-n Taylor approximation using the Lagrange remainder formula and a bound on the (n+1)th derivative.
question_archetypes.example: Find P_7(x) for e^x and use Taylor's Theorem to confirm P_7(1) gives e correct to 3 decimals.
question_archetypes.answer: E_7(1) = e^s/8! for some 0<s<1, so E_7(1) < e/40320 < 3/40320 ≈ 0.0000744 < 0.0005, confirming 3-decimal accuracy
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question asks to guarantee a certain accuracy or confirm correct decimal places — requires bounding |f^(n+1)(s)| over the relevant interval (not evaluating it exactly, since s is unknown) and plugging into the Lagrange remainder formula.
method_plan: Compute f^(n+1)(x) symbolically
Find a bound K for |f^(n+1)(s)| valid for all s between a and the target x
Substitute into E_n(x) = f^(n+1)(s)/(n+1)! * (x-a)^(n+1) to get |E_n(x)| <= K/(n+1)! * |x-a|^(n+1)
Compare the resulting bound to the required precision
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct (n+1)th derivative found
M1: correct bound K on |f^(n+1)(s)| over the relevant interval
A1: correct final error bound computed
A1: correct conclusion about the requested accuracy

common_errors.description: Attempting to evaluate f^(n+1)(s) exactly, forgetting that s is an unknown point — only a BOUND on |f^(n+1)| can be used
Factorial or arithmetic slip in the remainder formula

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a Taylor polynomial already found (by any method), write down the correct Lagrange remainder E_n(x) expression for it, without necessarily evaluating a numeric bound.
question_archetypes.example: Find the 3rd-order Maclaurin polynomial for f(x)=ln(1+2x), and give the Lagrange remainder form for E_3(x).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question specifically asks for the FORM of the remainder (not a numeric bound), testing whether the student can correctly identify n, differentiate one more time than the polynomial's degree, and write the Lagrange expression with the correct unknown point s.
method_plan: Identify n from the given polynomial's degree
Differentiate f one more time (to order n+1) to get f^(n+1)(t)
Write E_n(x) = f^(n+1)(s)/(n+1)! * (x-a)^(n+1), with s an unspecified point between a and x
State clearly that s is unknown (not equal to a or x)
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct identification of n and the needed order of differentiation
M1: correct (n+1)th derivative computed
A1: correctly assembled remainder expression with the unspecified s

common_errors.description: Writing the remainder with s replaced by a or by x, rather than leaving it as a general unspecified point
Differentiation error finding f^(n+1)(t) for a composite function like ln(1+2x)

micro_skills.subtopic: Using Known Maclaurin Series (Substitution Shortcuts and Limit Evaluation)
micro_skills.micro_skill: Find Taylor/Maclaurin polynomials via algebraic substitution into known series, and use series to evaluate indeterminate limits
definitions: f(x)=O(u(x)) as x->a means |f(x)|<=K|u(x)| near a for some constant K. Properties: O(u)+O(u)=O(u); C*O(u)=O(u); if f=O((x-a)^k u(x)) then f/(x-a)^k=O(u(x)).

theorems.name: Theorem 13 (uniqueness)
theorems.statement: If f(x)=Q_n(x)+O((x-a)^(n+1)) for a degree-<=n polynomial Q_n, then Q_n=P_n (the Taylor polynomial) — this lets Taylor polynomials be found by algebraic manipulation of known series instead of repeated differentiation.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Find P_n(x) about a nonzero point (or for a composite argument) by algebraically substituting into one of the six memorized Maclaurin series, invoking Theorem 13 rather than differentiating from scratch.
question_archetypes.example: Find P_3(x) for e^(2x) about x=1 using the Maclaurin series for e^t.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The function is built from a standard elementary function (e^t, sin t, 1/(1-t), etc.) composed with a linear or simple inner expression — substitute the inner expression into the known series rather than differentiating the composite function repeatedly.
method_plan: Rewrite the function so the known series' variable t equals a simple expression in (x-a)
Substitute into the memorized Maclaurin series for that elementary function
Collect terms up to the required order, expressing everything as powers of (x-a)
Invoke Theorem 13 to conclude this IS the Taylor polynomial P_n
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct rewriting isolating the substitution variable t in terms of (x-a)
M1: correct substitution into the known series
A1: correctly collected terms up to the required order
A1: correct final P_n(x) with justification via Theorem 13

common_errors.description: Substituting incorrectly, e.g. using x instead of (x-a) as the series variable when expanding about a nonzero point
Error expanding a power like [2(x-1)]^3, mishandling the constant factor

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Evaluate an indeterminate limit by expanding numerator and denominator in Taylor series to a sufficiently high order (an alternative to repeated l'Hopital's Rule), until the leading surviving terms give a determinate ratio.
question_archetypes.example: Evaluate lim_{x->0} (2 sin(x) - sin(2x)) / (2e^x - 2 - 2x - x^2).
question_archetypes.answer: 3 (numerator = x^3+O(x^5), denominator = x^3/3+O(x^4), ratio -> x^3/(x^3/3) = 3)
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The limit's numerator and denominator both individually expand to 0 at low orders in their series (i.e., naive low-order expansion still gives 0/0) — must expand to at least ONE order past where the leading terms first cancel.
method_plan: Expand each piece of the numerator and denominator as Maclaurin series to a generous order
Combine and simplify, canceling terms that vanish, until the leading nonzero term of each is found
Form the ratio of leading terms
State the limit; if it's still 0/0 at the chosen order, redo with one more order of expansion
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct series expansions of each piece to a sufficient order
M1: correct simplification identifying the leading surviving term in numerator and denominator
A1: correct final limit from the ratio of leading terms

common_errors.description: Using a Taylor polynomial of too-low order, so all surviving terms cancel to 0/0 again instead of revealing the true limit
Arithmetic error combining/canceling terms across the two series expansions

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Distinguish correctly between a 'Taylor polynomial about a' and a 'Maclaurin polynomial', and between truncation error and the specific O(...) notation used to track it.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why the expansion of cos(x) given in the standard memorized list is called a Maclaurin series, and what changes if the same function were expanded about x=pi instead.
question_archetypes.answer: A Maclaurin polynomial/series is specifically a Taylor polynomial/series about a=0; expanding cos(x) about x=pi instead would require computing cos(pi), -sin(pi), etc. as the new coefficients, giving a genuinely different (though related) polynomial in powers of (x-pi).
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The question is explicitly conceptual/terminological (asking to explain or distinguish) rather than computational — common on exams as a quick conceptual check alongside computational Taylor problems.
method_plan: State the general definition of a Taylor polynomial about a
State that 'Maclaurin' specifically means a=0
Contrast what changes (the coefficients, expressed in powers of (x-a)) when a≠0
Give a concrete brief illustration if requested
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct general definition stated
A1: correct identification that Maclaurin = Taylor about 0
A1: correct illustrative contrast for a≠0

common_errors.description: Using 'Taylor polynomial' and 'Maclaurin polynomial' as fully interchangeable terms regardless of the expansion point
Giving only a definition without the requested illustrative contrast

micro_skills.topic: Roundoff Error, Truncation Error, and Computers
micro_skills.subtopic: Distinguishing Truncation Error from Roundoff Error
micro_skills.micro_skill: Distinguish truncation error from roundoff error and identify which dominates in a given numerical scenario
definitions: Truncation error is the error from cutting off an infinite/exact process after finitely many terms (e.g. discarding a Taylor remainder) — a mathematical approximation error present even with infinite-precision arithmetic.
Roundoff error is the error from a computer's finite-precision (floating-point) representation of real numbers (mantissa x base^exponent with finitely many bits).
Machine epsilon is the smallest positive floating-point number such that the computer recognizes 1+epsilon>1; for a typical 64-bit double, epsilon=2^(-52)≈2.22e-16.

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Estimate the truncation error in approximating a function value by a specific-order Maclaurin polynomial, using the Lagrange remainder, independent of any computer arithmetic.
question_archetypes.example: Estimate the truncation error in approximating sin(0.1) by its degree-3 Maclaurin polynomial P_3(x)=x-x^3/6.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The problem asks specifically about the error from stopping a series/polynomial at a finite order — a pure truncation-error question, independent of what machine or arithmetic system evaluates the result.
method_plan: Identify the Lagrange remainder formula for the given order n
Bound the (n+1)th derivative over the relevant interval
Compute the resulting truncation error bound
State that this bound is independent of computer arithmetic
full_mark_rubric: M1: correct remainder formula identified for the given order
M1: correct bound on the (n+1)th derivative
A1: correct final truncation-error bound

common_errors.description: Confusing this bound with roundoff error and attributing it to the computer's precision instead of the mathematical truncation

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Given a numerical computation scenario, determine whether truncation error or roundoff error is the dominant source of inaccuracy, and explain how each could be reduced.
question_archetypes.example: A calculation approximates a function extremely close to the expansion point a using a high-order Taylor polynomial; explain why roundoff error, not truncation error, becomes dominant here.
question_archetypes.answer: As x approaches a, the truncation error (proportional to (x-a)^(n+1)) shrinks toward zero very quickly, but the floating-point roundoff error from representing and combining the (still finite-precision) terms does not shrink at the same rate — so roundoff becomes the limiting factor, not truncation.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The scenario describes a situation where truncation error is already very small (close to the expansion point, or a very high polynomial order) — a cue that the dominant remaining error must be attributed to roundoff instead.
method_plan: Identify how truncation error behaves in the given scenario (shrinking with order n or with proximity to a)
Recognize that roundoff error is governed by machine epsilon and does not depend on n or proximity to a in the same way
Conclude which source dominates and justify
State how each type of error could independently be reduced (more terms/closer to a for truncation; higher-precision arithmetic for roundoff)
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct description of truncation error's behavior in the scenario
A1: correct description of roundoff error's independent behavior
M1: correct conclusion identifying the dominant source with justification

common_errors.description: Using 'roundoff error' and 'truncation error' interchangeably, not recognizing they have distinct causes and remedies
Identifying the dominant source without explaining WHY (i.e. without contrasting how each error behaves)

question_archetypes.prompt_template: Explain why subtracting two nearly-equal floating-point numbers (catastrophic cancellation) can amplify roundoff error, using a numerical example.
question_archetypes.example: Explain why computing (1-cos(x))/x^2 directly for very small x on a computer can give an inaccurate result, and how rewriting the expression can help.
question_archetypes.answer: For very small x, cos(x) is extremely close to 1, so 1-cos(x) involves subtracting two nearly-equal floating-point numbers, and most of their significant digits cancel, leaving a result dominated by roundoff error; rewriting using a Taylor/trig identity (e.g. (1-cos x)/x^2 -> using sin^2(x/2) forms) avoids this direct cancellation.
question_archetypes.recognition_cue: The computation involves subtracting two quantities that are very close in value (especially for small or extreme parameter values) — a classic setup for catastrophic cancellation amplifying roundoff error well beyond machine epsilon.
method_plan: Identify the subtraction of two nearly-equal quantities in the computation
Explain how this cancels significant digits, amplifying the relative roundoff error
Propose an algebraically equivalent rewrite that avoids the direct subtraction
State why the rewritten form is more numerically stable
full_mark_rubric: A1: correct identification of the near-equal subtraction causing cancellation
M1: correct explanation of why this amplifies roundoff error
A1: correct alternative, more stable rewriting proposed

common_errors.description: Attributing the resulting inaccuracy to truncation error rather than roundoff/cancellation
Not proposing any algebraic remedy, only describing the problem
